speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: TRIBUTES ON PASSING OF MEMBER FOR HULL
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the House will be saddened to learn, as I was saddened and distressed to learn, of the passing this morning of our colleague the hon. Member for Hull, Alexis Caron, a friend and valued comrade over the years and, for a time, my Parliamentary Secretary.
Mr. Caron, as we all know, was a man of kindness and generosity with an alert understanding of human nature, its weaknesses and its strength. He was a very great individualist, an unyielding and eloquent fighter for those causes and principles in which he believed; a man of sturdy independence, a man who served his country and his party well; he was whip of our party in the House for some years, as hon. Members know. He served his city as Mayor. He served his province as a member of the legislature to which he was first elected, I believe, in 1935. And he served his country as a member of this Parliament, always with diligence and honour, over many years.
He will be very greatly missed. We knew he was in indifferent health but his death came both as a surprise and a shock, and I should like to extend to his wife, Mrs. Caron, and to his family our very deep and heartfelt sympathy.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of the Opposition):

Mr. Speaker, it is on occasions such as this that we in the House of Commons, separated by party considerations, realize we have so much in common; a relationship that is only possible in a democracy, a relationship between those who disagree with each other politically that does not cause our friendships to be limited by the places in the House in which we may sit.
I join with the Prime Minister in the expression of deep sorrow on the passing of Alexis Caron, a man who, as was stated by the Prime Minister, served in all fields of public life; as Mayor of his city, as a Member
of the Provincial Legislature, and as a Member of the House of Commons for many years. He was a man of strong personal feelings, one who expressed himself in a way that could be understood and with equal facility in both languages on those matters about which he felt keenly. The Prime Minister said he was a man of independent thought and action. I think that describes him very well. He regarded his position as a party follower as not inconsistent with a degree of independence when decisions were made with which he was not in full agreement.
On behalf of Her Majesty's Loyal Opposition we join with the Prime Minister in extending our sympathy to the widow and members of the family, as well as to the Prime Minister and the associates and confreres of Mr. Caron for so many years in this Chamber.

speechtext:
1.	What research projects is the government and its agencies undertaking with regard to pollution studies and surveys, and causes of and remedies for pollution in the great lakes?
2.	What other bodies, corporations or agencies are studying this problem?
3.	What sums (itemize) has the government considered for the above projects?
4.	What boards or commissions have direct or indirect control or interest in pollution in the great lakes and what are their programs?
5.	Are any of the following techniques contemplated by the government to encourage industry to curb pollution (a) special research grants for studies to avoid pollution (b) tax incentive to build or counteract pollution control systems on industrial work beds (c) civil action against industries discharging pollutants?

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean-Luc Pepin (Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys):
speakerposition: Minister of Mines and Technical Surveys
subtopic: STUDIES OF GREAT LAKES POLLUTION
speechtext:
1. There is a coordinated plan of research, by agencies of the Canadian government and government of the province of Ontario, concerning pollution of the great lakes. In general, the federal government is directing its studies toward the body of the lakes and the cause and distribution of pollution that does or may cross the international boundary. The Ontario agencies are
primarily concerned with the origins of pollution on land, their effects in the great lakes and their control.
Specific federal government studies include the circulation of the water; properties of the water including chemical impurities, their concentration and probable destination; rate of mixing and diffusion in the lakes; the effect of nutrient chemicals (phosphates, nitrates, etc.) on the excessive growth of algae (eutrophication) and means of alleviating such eutrophication; study of the health hazards from domestic sewage and other wastes originating on land or in boats and means of its control.
2.	The Ontario Water Resources Commission is the body primarily responsible for water pollution control under Ontario laws. It conducts research to define the sources and kinds of pollution entering the lakes from industry, municipalities, agricultural drainage and small boats, the distribution of this pollution and the properties of such pollutants and their control. Under the International Joint Commission reference this work has been expanded with financial aid from the federal government.
The Great Lakes Institute of the University of Toronto is conducting surveillance surveys and special research studies of the great lakes under contracts and grants from the Department of Mines and Technical Surveys, the Fisheries Research Board, National Research Council, and the Ontario Water Resources Commission. It is provided with transportation in the ship Port Dauphine by the Department of Transport.
Other agencies: In the United States, many federal and state agencies and universities are conducting programs on the lakes, related to pollution and other scientific studies. Among them, major activities are in progress by the department of the interior, federal water pollution control administration; the U.S. lake survey; and the U.S. bureau of commercial fisheries. The University of Michigan, Great Lakes Research Division is a major contributor among the universities. Activities by the individual states are increasing but are somewhat limited, as yet.
Through direct contact with the above agencies, by liaison through the International Joint Commission and by scientific meetings, exchange of information and program planning are ach;eved on an international basis.
3.	During the current fiscal year the funds supporting great lakes investigations are: Department of Mines and Technical Surveys.

$800,000; Fisheries Research Board, $250,000; National Health and Welfare, $300,000; International Joint Commission, $308,000.
Under cost sharing, the Ontario Water Resources Commission is reimbursed through the Canadian section of the International Joint Commission for approximately 50 percent of their costs. Expenditures for subsequent years have not been critically considered by the government and itemized sums are not available. It can be anticipated, however, that sharply increased amounts of money will be required in both the operating and capital votes to meet federal responsibilities.
4.	The International Joint Commission. The governments of the United States and Canada referred the following questions to the International Joint Commission for investigation and report:
Are the waters of lake Erie, lake Ontario and the international section of the St. Lawrence river being polluted on either side of the boundary to an extent which is causing or is likely to cause injury to health or property on the other side? If so, to what extent, by what causes and in what localities? What remedial measures would, in its judgment, be most practicable and what would be the probable cost?
The International Joint Commission established the international lake Erie water pollution board and the international lake On-tario-St. Lawrence river water pollution board to undertake, through appropriate agencies in Canada and the United States, the necessary investigations and studies. Canadian members of the boards are officials of the Departments of National Health and Welfare, Mines and Technical Surveys, Fisheries and the Ontario Water Resources Commission. United States members similarly are federal and state officials. The boards drew up a coordinated program of the investigations, surveys and studies required to answer the questions referred to the International Joint Commission, together with an allocation of the work among the several participating agencies to avoid duplication of effort. This program was approved by the commission and, in Canada, is being carried out by the individual agencies and departments as described herein. Co-ordination of activities in both countries is achieved through these boards, which report periodically to the International Joint Commission.
[Mr. Pepin.1
Federal government agencies having an interest in pollution in the great lakes, and their programs are:
Department of Mines and Technical Surveys: Three branches of this department, the marine sciences branch, the water research branch and the geological survey branch are co-operating in the current year's program. This department is concerned with studies of the main body of lake Ontario and to a lesser extent lake Erie, concerning the physical and chemical characteristics of the water. This includes investigations of circulation, and current patterns, mixing and diffusion of pollutants, temperature distribution, bottom sediments-water interface relations, air-water interface phenomena, seismic and airborne geophysical techniques.
The Fisheries Research Board of Canada, under the Minister of Fisheries, which is conducting research on eutrophication of lakes (i.e. the changes brought about by enrichment from pollutants) and means of controlling it.
The Department of National Health and Welfare is conducting research on the health hazards of various pollutants, their sources and distribution in natural waters, and the means whereby they can be suitably treated or otherwise controlled.
The National Research Council through its associate committee on water pollution research is promoting research in universities on specific water pollution problems and the means of improving abatement measures and assessing the significance of pollutants in water; is encouraging training of people in pollution control technology, and is encouraging industry to conduct research and control of pollution from industrial sources.
The Canadian committee on water pollution, formed in February, 1966 by direction of the Privy Council office, provides a forum where federal and provincial agencies can exchange information, co-ordinate their efforts and ensure that all necessary research is being properly planned.
The United States-Canadian great lakes study group is a committee of United States-Canadian engineers and scientists who meet semi-annually to review and co-ordinate all programs dealing with studies in the great lakes.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE

speechtext: The house resumed, from Tuesday, August 30, consideration of the motion of Mr. Pearson for the second reading of Bill No. 230, to provide for the resumption of operations of railways and for the settlement of the existing dispute with respect to terms and conditions of employment between railway companies and their employees, and on the amendment thereto of Mr. Diefenbaker.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR RESUMPTION OF RAILWAY OPERATIONS AND SETTLEMENT OF LABOUR DISPUTE
speechtext:
In rising today to take part in the debate on the bill now before the house I hope I can make some small contribution toward a solution of this serious problem which is facing the country today. I hope that perhaps in some small way I can influence someone on the government side to take a second look at the measure which is before us and make some reasonable changes in it.
As I speak today, I am not speaking, as the phrase goes, off the top of my head. I am speaking as a railroader with 25 years of active experience on the railroad. I am also speaking as a representative of one of the unions involved in the strike today-the operating union, the Brotherhood of Railway Trainmen. I was a representative for them for 15 years, and their representative in matters of legislation for four years. I have been closely associated with the railroads and with the unions throughout my period of service in the industry, so I think I can speak with some authority on the railroad problem and on what the railroaders are thinking today.
I shall be a little kinder to the railway companies than was my colleague, the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) who stated, in effect, I believe, that the railway companies did not negotiate. I would say that I deplore the very negative approach they take toward collective bargaining. I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that in making this statement I am being very kind to them.
There is clear evidence of this negative approach in the fact that this is the fourth time the government has had to intervene in railroad labour-management disputes. It is also proof that the railroads are not approaching collective bargaining in the same manner as collective bargaining is generally carried on between industry and labour. This
August 31, 1966
7880	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters has been my experience both as a railroader and as a union man.
I listened with great interest to the hon. member for Verdun (Mr. Mackasey) last night. He spoke with sincerity. I would have to agree with a good part of what he said, but I cannot be as optimistic as the hon. member in respect to the railroads sincerely getting down again to negotiations with the unions in order to bring about a better settlement. This legislation contains no hope of that. I am satisfied the railroad companies are going to stand pat and take their chances on arbitration. This may be a personal opinion, but my experience with the unions gives me a good foundation for making that statement.
I would also like to tell the hon. member for Verdun that it is not a matter of the railroaders not properly understanding the provisions of Bill C-230. Rather, it is a case of their understanding too well the attitude of the railway companies in the matter of collective bargaining. This is the problem. They have no faith in the companies resuming negotiations and giving them any more than is outlined in this bill.
The hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) said one of the problems in the railroad industry concerned the lessening gap in the pay structures for skilled and unskilled workers. I am quite sure my colleague did not intend no imply that the so-called unskilled workers are overpaid. The point he was trying to make was that the pay differential between skilled and unskilled workers was not enough. In this connection I do not think the railroads are fair in classifying skilled and unskilled workers. I feel certain many unskilled workers could be classified as highly skilled workers.
My experience lay in the operating field, but my sympathy goes out to the non-ops because I believe they have suffered more discrimination in the matter of inadequate pay. The problems of the operating groups are numerous, but they are different from those of the non-ops.
The section foreman is one of the most important people on a railroad, yet in a sense he is looked down upon, even though there is no more hard working man in the industry. He must acquire a good understanding of basic engineering. He is responsible for the proper elevation of tracks and other work which, if not done properly, could contribute to accidents, injuries and possibly death. Yet his take-home pay is a national disgrace. All through the years these people have been


deprived of a proper income. Many of them are now being pensioned off and because of their low rate of pay their pensions are totally inadequate.
Railroad bridge and building crews are also highly skilled workmen. They build bridges. They do all the heavy work in the construction. They maintain them. They build houses and even do cabinet making. I believe their services are not recognized in the proper manner.
I can give an example of their wage rate. One constituent of mine was with the C.N.R. bridge and building section. He took his pension two years earlier than required and got a job in construction which paid him $1.78 more per hour than he was paid when working on the railroad, plus $2.60 a day travelling expenses. This is adequate proof that the railroaders are underpaid. Freight and express workmen are another group which is badly underpaid. I can cite the case of an express clerk who is married and is trying to rear his family on take-home pay of less than $300 a month. Another clerk with 15 years seniority has take-home pay of approximately $280 per month, and he is a marrried man with five children. Is it any wonder that such people are hostile when they think the government would consider such a measly increase as is offered in this bill?
I quite understand that hon. members on the other side of the house have said that this is an open-end formula, that it involves only an interim payment; but from my experience in negotiations with the railroads I have a strong feeling that, if the bill passes unamended, it will be many months before the workers get an additional raise. The increase offered by the bill is meagre and does not alleviate the position in which railroaders find themselves today.
Railroaders are the most maligned of people. No others in industry have been criticized so much for feather-bedding; yet it is rather odd that railroaders are being made redundant and can still be responsible for a national crisis because they walk off their jobs.
I do not wish to take the time of the house to explain the pay structure of the operating crafts. No one would be much the wiser if I did because it is one of the most complex formulae to be found anywhere. In it there is real inequality. I agree that many of the operating people, if they hold good positions in freight or passenger service, can make a reasonably good monthly wage. But by the
August 31, 1966	COMMONS
same token there are many more who, due to the complex wage structure, are subject to very low wages if they do not have the seniority required in order to hold a decent job.
[DOT] (3:50 p.m.)
Just as an example, while these men work on a mileage basis, if they are working on jobs where mileage does not accumulate and where there is less road mileage than 100 miles involved, their rate is $2.09 an hour. Under circumstances where a man is forced on a job, I think this is a very unrealistic wage in this day and age. If he works on a run of over 100 miles, he is paid by the mile and receives $16.35 for every 100 miles. This inequality does not exist because the men want it. It does not exist because the unions have not tried to do something about it. It exists became every time the unions attempt to have something done about it the company will go along with the discussion but will not do anyth ng about it. They do not want to bring the poorly paid man up to the rate of the better paid man: They want to bring the better paid man down to the level of the lower paid man. This is the only time they want to negotiate on this.
Time after time our unions have tried to do something about this inequality and bring about a more simplified pay structure. The companies are more concerned with trying to cut the wages of the higher paid workers, and therefore they never get off the ground so far as this particular subject is concerned. The yard conductor switchman always works on an hourly basis. His rate is $2.66 an hour. I would say that on the average a yard conductor's service with the company would be anywhere from 20 to 40 years. When a man has put in 20 to 40 years on a job, has the skills required to perform that job properly and is required to take the responsibility for the involvement of machines worth hundreds of thousands of dollars and goods worth hundreds of thousands of dollars, I think $2.66 an hour is absolutely outrageous. When you add the 6 per cent on to that it is hardly worth mentioning.
Last night I listened with interest to the Minister of National Health and Welfare. He too seemed to be optimistic that when the chips were down the companies would sit down to negotiate. I should like to remind the Minister of National Health and Welfare that at the time a unanimous report of a conciliation board was more or less forced down the

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters company's throat, this was government intervention too. Even though the conciliation board was unanimous in recommending a formula for settlement, the company would have no part of it, and at this time too it almost resulted in a crisis.
Therefore, I must reiterate what I said before. I am not optimistic that if this bill is passed there will be any very decided improvement for the workers for a great time to come. I can see months of delay and frustration while the men get more bitter all the time.
I should like to refer also to what the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Thompson) said with regard to the Freedman commission report-that is, that the recommendations of the Freedman commission report should be referred for negotiation between the companies and the unions. I am not criticizing the hon. member for Red Deer, because as is the case in respect of a majority of people, I am quite sure he does not understand that the only reason there was a wildcat strike on the Canadian National Railways is that the unions for years have tried to have written into their contract the same things that are recommended by the Freedman commission report. In this regard they have not met with any success. This is the only reason there was a wildcat strike on the Canadian National Railways.
This time again, when the unions and the company were trying to negotiate there was a proposal from the unions that the recommendations of the Freedman report be part of the contract. The company turned thumbs down on it; they absolutely will not negotiate. The only way it is going to be put into effect is by government legislation; make no mistake about that.
Like all union members I am opposed to compulsory arbitration. I do not think it solves anything. If we ever get to the point where all these disputes go to compulsory arbitration, management will not settle at any time; they will sit back and gamble in the hope that when it goes to compulsory arbitration they will get the best of the deal. Without criticizing arbitrators, our people do not have confidence that when the company goes to arbitration it does not get a little the best of the deal. This is another thing which is bugging the railroaders today.
The point I wish to make most clear is the fact that it is not because the railroader does not understand Bill C-230 that he is so upset today. It is because he does understand how
August 31, 1966

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters the companies have been negotiating for the past 16 years since the strike of 1950. It is my opinion that never since 1950 have the companies sat down and negotiated in good faith. Perhaps there has been some token negotiating, with the understanding in the back of their minds that eventually there would be government intervention and that if there is government intervention they would have the government on the spot; either the taxpayers would have to pick up the tab or the government would have to step in and relieve them of some of the burden which they find, or pretend to find, too heavy to bear.
I am not going to argue the point about inability to pay. I recognize the fact that railroads perhaps are not in as favourable a position as is most industry when they have to provide additional wages. I should like to say very strongly, however, that I do not think the Canadian Pacific Railway has a good argument in respect of inability to pay. So far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned, if they were not burdened with an unrealistic debt which I think costs in the neighbourhood of $60 or $70 million a year in interest, I feel they could not plead inability to pay either.
To a great extent the position the railways find themselves in today is their own fault. It is only in the past few years that the railways have got off their behinds-if you do not mind my saying that-and have tried to modernize. They wanted to sit there and let somebody else carry the burden for them. I do have a little optimism. In the past few years I think they have tried to get back into the transportation field and have tried to compete on a fair basis. However, I still suggest that the railways can blame themselves to a great extent if there is inability to pay today, so far as railroad operation is concerned.
Mr. Speaker, from the start I never intended to take up too much of the time of the house. I should like to say something in conclusion, and if this gets out to a lot of the union men I might not be too popular with them. I should like to have it clearly understood, however, that I do not in any way subscribe to defiance of the law, under any circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was not my intention to take part in this debate at the very beginning, but as it apears that it will be longer than expected, I will take a few minutes to state part of my views and also add to the sauce offered to us by the government as well as the opposition. I would like to add some spice to the main speech delivered by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). After hearing the voice of those two parliamentary leaders, we finally have a rather tasteless and stale sauce. Perhaps another cook might improve the taste.
The more I consider the attitude of the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) and that of the Leader of the Official Opposition, the more I find they are the same.
When we take the time to read carefully the speech delivered by the Prime Minister in favour of the bill before us, we are carried back a few years when a similar situation occurred and the argumentation of the government in office to settle the problems at that time was put forward.
As for the Leader of the Opposition, he does exactly the same thing. He gives us a history lesson, the conclusion reached is that what the other has done at the time he was either in the opposition or in power. After the history lesson, the conclusion reached is that when they are on the government side, they are both the same, and when they are on the
August 31, 1966	COMMONS
opposition side, they are also both the same. To protect the rights of the workers, their interests, their welfare, both were better in opposition. Mr. Speaker, why do we not take these two parties and put them where they would be most productive, both in opposition, and bring to power a third party that would come up with a settlement once and for all, since both of them are better in opposition and since, when they change sides in the house, they also change their argument as easily as they change their shirt.
That is the problem and it never changes, but that will not truly solve the problem facing the country today. It was bypassed in the past and there will be more pussyfooting about without a final settlement. If the necessary measures, if effective and essential measures were taken to settle the problem of the railroad workers' strike, the same formula could possibly be applied to settle the many other strikes with which the country is faced at the present time. Such, Mr. Speaker, are my observations not only as concerns this discussion, on this particular bill, but ever since I have had the opportunity of sitting in this house.

The railway strike affects all spheres of the Canadian economy and productivity. We must ask ourselves why this strike is taking place and why the many other recent strikes have taken place. We must realize that more strikes are imminent because we are travelling a vicious circle. As salaries are increased the cost of living increases, and this is inevitably followed by more strikes for higher wages to compensate for the rise in costs. This cost of living is spiralling higher and higher and we have no idea when it will stop.
Provincial governments are not happy about the situation. I am sure that if this situation existed 50 or 60 years ago counterparts of men like Mr. Ross Thatcher would have come to Ottawa with six-guns to settle these problems with the prime minister. Housewives all over the country would like to go after the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) with rolling pins because of the high cost of living.
Why does the Prime Minister not have solutions to these problems? Perhaps it is because he spends his time looking for more peace prizes. I do not know what the Prime Minister intends to do to correct the existing situation, but I do know something has to be done. Let me add my grain of salt to this sauce in the hope that it will gain some

Legislation Respecting Railway Matters flavour. Let me express my opinions in the hope that the government will pay attention and find in part at least some answer to the difficult problems which now face us.
Let us consider what the railway employees think about the bill now before us. Apparently it does not satisfy them to any great extent because it does not grapple with the problem. Some of the men on strike do not particularly want an increase in income, but would like an improvement in working conditions and facilities. Another group does want an increase in salary and is not particularly concerned about working conditions. Perhaps part of the reason for this difference of opinion relates to the various classifications in which groups of railway employees find themselves. No one can convince me that the means and needs of the presidents, vice presidents, executive vice presidents and managers are the same as the means and needs of the common section workers, station agents, ticket collectors or switchmen. They are in different categories. They might not have the same needs. We have not distinguished between these two classes of workers. There is the labouring section, part of which needs higher wages. We are offering these men 6 per cent, which is probably not enough. But if this 6 per cent were applied in the right quarters, it would be enough and the cost to the government would not be any greater. In this event 6 per cent would probably be sufficient and would satisfy the workers who need better working conditions but not necessarily higher wages.
[DOT] (4:10 p.m.)
I have in mind the trainman sitting in the caboose at the back of a freight train. Do you realize, Mr. Speaker, that these men still have the same living quarters that they had when the first train was run in Canada? They have not any toilet facilities, except the open air; the back end of the train is used for this purpose. If it is too cold and these men have to use whatever facilities there are inside the caboose, I do not know what they do.
Coal-oil lamps are used on these trains; the companies will not tolerate any kind of generator being used. The lamp is taken out to work by the trainman and he takes it back when he returns to the shop. On some of the super continental trains the cook is running around in a little space perhaps 5 feet wide and 15 feet long for 8 or 10 hours a day. He is preparing 700 or 1,000 meals a day. Where are his sleeping quarters? He sleeps on top of
August 31. 1966
7884	COMMONS
Legislation Respecting Railway Matters a dining-room table or in the baggage compartment with a couple of hens or pigs to keep him company, and the pigs are grunting all night.
These are examples of the working conditions of some of the men employed on the railways. Another type of railway worker leaves the station with his packsack, overcoat, flashlight and lantern. If he had to carry all this equipment once or twice a year, it wouldn't be too bad; but he does this two or three times a week over a period of perhaps 30 years. When these men are working around the station they are not able to walk between the cars; they have to crawl underneath the train. The cars are not separated, and as a result this worker has to crawl underneath them carrying all his gear. It would not be too much trouble to separate them and allow the workers to walk between the cars.
This is what I mean when I refer to bad working conditions; and these conditions can be improved. A raise in salary will not improve the working conditions of the man working on the freight train who is forced to use open air toilet facilities at a temperature of perhaps 40 degrees below zero, in broad daylight. If there were a reclassification of jobs, and working conditions were improved, you could give an increase in salary to the men who need it, and better working conditions to those who need them. In my opinion more railway workers would be satisfied if this were done. This is one aspect of the problem that the government and the commission provided for in the bill, if it is ever passed, should stress, namely improved working conditions and equitable, just remuneration.
I am worried about this 6 per cent because, as always, this money comes from the Canadian citizen in the form of taxes. The government may well be worried about inflation at the moment because every time they increase wages to settle a strike, whether it be on the railroad or anywhere else, the cost of living immediately increases. If the government is worried about inflation, why do they not take other measures to solve the situation? If one course can only lead to disaster, why not take another? Good grief, Mr. Speaker, there must be other measures that could be taken. There must be men in the government capable of working out a more satisfactory course. When hon. members opposite go around the city, they change direction. Why don't they do the same thing in order to solve our economic problems,


whether they be connected with operating a railroad or a country. It does not surprise me that we have strikes, because this government cannot even operate the parking area on parliament hill. If this is so, how can we expect them to run a railroad?
Instead of giving just 6 per cent to workers who need a higher increase, and hollering and yelling to the country that they cannot give any more because of inflation, the government should have considered this result when they came out with the 11 per cent tax on building materials. The cost of living went up as a result of that tax, and it will probably go up after we have dealt with the bank legislation this fall. In the minister's bill there is no limit on the interest rate chargeable on loans. The government raise the ceiling on interest. These things increase the cost of living, but we have not as yet had a strike in the banks. I know railroad men who work in shacks, but every bank manager I know has a big office in which to work. If the money obtained from increased interest were used to raise the salary of bank employees, I would not say a word; but I know where this money is going.
Raising the ceiling on interest rates has increased the cost of living, but the government does not talk about inflation when dealing with the financial sector of the economy. However, to the worker they say, "Be satisfied. Don't complain too much, because a salary increase will cause inflation." This is the sing-song we have been listening to for years, and it is about time the government changed its attitude in this respect. They should try shooting with the right arm instead of the left. If they did this they might hit the target sometimes.
To improve our economy in the future the government will have to divide the public part of the economy from the private. Until they do this they will be faced with a wall of trouble every day. Our interest on our national debt is about $1 billion a year. Doesn't this contribute to inflation? What does it add up to per capita in Canada? The government should finance the public sector of the economy interest free, or at operational cost. This might very much reduce the tax paid by Canadian citizens. Every time the government imposes a tax, the cost of living goes up.
The job of this government is to see that the needs of every individual are met. Not only must we improve production but we must improve the ability of the individual to
August 31, 1966	COMMONS
purchase that production. In my opinion the government has failed to realize this aspect of the problem. They must see that the purchasing power of the Canadian people is at all times not more or less than the goods we are producing. If a proper balance is not maintained in this regard you will have either inflation or deflation. If you have inflation, you are off-balance, so get back into balance and take measures to achieve this end.
When I speak of the public sector of the economy I refer to the financing of bridges, railroads, schools, roads and projects undertaken by municipalities and provincial governments. When any level of government wishes to undertake a public project, it should be financed interest free because these governments are providing a service to the country. This is not production but it is a service from which the producing, private sector of the economy benefits.
After a road has been built it begins to depreciate, but we pay interest on the total amount of money originally borrowed to build the road. This is what causes inflation. You build a road; it costs $1 million and you commence repaying the loan. Immediately after the road has been built, it depreciates. You borrow $1 million to build the road, you pay interest at perhaps 5 per cent for 20 years and at the end of that period you have, in effect, paid for two roads because you have repaid the original loan of $1 million and the interest has amounted to $1 million. That is $2 million for the basic value of a $1 million road. There is inflation there and by the time the road is paid for it has outgrown its usefulness. To whom is the interest paid? I would like the Minister of Finance (Mr. Sharp) or the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) to get up and tell us to whom this interest is paid. We may then start on the road to success and not on the road to bankruptcy, which is so often the case-or the road to credit restriction.

On May 31 of last year when I told the Minister of Finance, when he reduced the reserves in the chartered banks from 8 per cent to 7 per cent, that he was the originator of the restriction he called me a prophet. I would like the minister to refer back to the words I said on May 31, 1965. Maybe I was a prophet; but he was a fool. This may not be parliamentary language but it is still common sense. All we have here is common sense, and I think we realize that very well.

If I were to go to a bank to borrow money so as to continue the production of my company, the interest would not be included in the cost price. Now, Mr. Speaker, in view of what I have said I wish to present to this house the following subamendment, seconded by the hon. member for Roberval (Mr. Gauthier):

As I say, I wish to set out as clearly as I can, and as unprovocatively and objectively as I can, the purposes and objectives we had in mind in this legislation and in the policy which is responsible for this legislation. I think it is important to do this, Mr. Speaker, because of misinterpretations which have been given-as I believe them to have been misinterpretations-and wrong interpretations which have been made-as I believe them to have been wrong-with respect to the meaning of the legislation and its clauses, which in my view could have the effect of misleading and confusing those who under this bill would be required to resume their duties.

That is if the bill secures second reading; if it does not, that is a very different matter and the measure before us disappears and, no doubt, the government with it.
I believe these misinterpretations I have mentioned are especially misleading with regard to the wage figures in the bill for 1966 which have been put forward as indicating that these are somehow the final figures, the final increase that these 120,000 men affected by the legislation can secure in the next two years.
Let me mention, Mr. Speaker-and I intend to be brief this evening-the objectives of the government in putting forward this legislation. The first, of course-and this is the reason we are here-is to get the railways into operation again with the least possible delay. Believe me, this is not our only problem in regard to railways. It has been pointed out during this debate that there are many things behind this particular emergency which must

I hope so.
The second objective is to assure the workers of an immediate increase in wages retroactive to January 1, 1966, not a final settlement but an immediate increase, provisional and tentative, to be adjusted by processes laid down in the legislation. I recognize, and I am sure all members in the house recognize, that the railway workers, to whom this country has owed so much ever since this country was formed and the first railways were built, are entitled to an increase in their wages. There is no difference of opinion about that.
Hear, hear.

The third objective is to interfere as little as possible with the normal process of free collective bargaining notwithstanding the emergency we face which has resulted in parliament intervening in this matter. I admit that much of this so-called process of free collective bargaining in recent years between the railways and their employees has been, as I think the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) described it, a kind of ritualistic dance. I know this is true, and this is one of the things we shall have to do something about. We have been saying so for a long time. Nevertheless the principle itself of free collective bargaining is worth affirming, even in this situation.
The fourth objective is to ensure that any agreement arrived at by the intervention of parliament through legislation, a procedure which is adopted only as a last resort, will be fair and reasonable to the workers affected by it and, of course, to the railways as well. Agreed.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Do I understand it is agreed that we continue until we have considered clauses 3, 4 and 5 and that at that time we will rise and report progress and have an order made by the house that we meet tomorrow at ten o'clock and continue through?
Agreed.
I do not wish to engage in any cross-fire with the Minister of Labour but he made some comments after my previous remarks to which I should like to refer.
On what clause?
Clause 3.

Clause 3 has been
carried.
[DOT] (12:10 a.m.)

It has not. I point out that in making his remarks the minister stated that in 1950 there was a similar clause in the act, and I was well aware of that. I have read the clause several times. Did the minister not read Prime Minister St. Laurent's statement that 1950 was not to be taken as a precedent? I do not believe that changing the word "return" to "resume" has eliminated the fact that 1950 is being taken as a precedent. I also point out that I do not agree that two wrongs make a right. I was not in this house in 1950 but I can assure you that, had I been, I would have taken the stand of Hon. David Croll on this matter now under discussion. Since two wrongs do not make a right, I would ask that we do the right thing in 1966 and that we do not forget the fact that we

DEBATES	August 31. 1966
are making a precedent out of an act which Mr. St. Laurent said was not to be taken as a precedent.
In addition, the minister points out that this clause is similar to one brought in in 1958. This is about the fourth time I have been told by members of the Liberal cabinet that they are doing something which is exactly the same as was done by the previous government. I ran in 1962 against the government of the day because I did not agree with its policies and I thought that the Liberals could do a better job. I ran against the same government in 1963 because I thought we could do a better job. There are quite a few Liberal members of this house who are getting fed up with hearing Liberal cabinet ministers tell us that this is just the way the previous government did things. Then why did we oppose them?
What is he like in caucus?

May I point out to you, Mr. Chairman, that Hon. David Croll said, as found on page 41 of Hansard for August 30, 1950:
Compulsion never removes the cause of the strife. Forced obedience against the will of those concerned sows the seeds of bitterness and resentment and in the end aggravates the very condition it was sought to cure.
I say to you, as members of the ministry, that it would be best to eliminate the words "employees now on strike shall resume the duties of their employment with the railway companies". Clause 4 will not need to be altered in any way and we will get rid of this forced labour or slavery clause. It does not affect clause 5. I sincerely ask the ministry to eliminate those words that will cause concern to the men now on strike, because I do not believe that that concern should be caused them.
The question has been asked by the Minister of Labour: What will happen if the men do not return to work? I could name a score of industries where the workers are on strike but which are still in business. They have engaged other employees. Are we going to force these men back to work because, when the railways announce that they are open for business, the men on strike may not go rushing back to the gates? I am opposed to compulsory labour.

Clause agreed to.
Clauses 4 and 5 agreed to.
Progress reported.
